result:
I think about windows.

Not the grand ones, not the stained glass or the tall museum windows that turn ordinary afternoons into something sacred. I mean the small, ordinary windows: the one that fogs when tea sits too long on the sill, the one that rattles in wind but never quite shakes itself loose, the one that opens a crack just enough to let the street noise in like a rumor.

A window is a promise that something outside still exists even when you can’t be there to feel it. It frames the world as if it were meant to be watched from a distance. You press your palm to the glass, and for a moment you are close enough to feel it warm, though you know the distance between your skin and the rain is only inches, yet it is also the whole distance between inside and outside.

I like the idea that every room contains a border we walk across without thinking. The chair by the window is where the room stops being only about you. The cat on the windowsill is not only a cat, but a small ambassador between worlds. The glass itself is a thin, transparent country: clear, quiet, full of reflected faces and passing trees.

There is something gentle about watching weather from inside. Rain becomes a story without dialogue. Snow becomes a page with no words, still and white, waiting to be read. Sunlight stretches across the floor like a yellow hand trying to reach something old and forgotten. The world is doing all of its loud, messy, beautiful work outside, and the window lets you share in it without having to step into the cold.

I also think about windows in old houses. The kind with too many panes, each one a little different, some slightly cracked, some clouded with age. They make every moment look as if it has been seen before. A bird outside becomes a memory. A passing car becomes a character. The whole day takes on the texture of something half-remembered, which is maybe how most of life actually feels: bright, but a little blurred at the edges.

If I could choose one small thing to spend a whole evening with, it would not be a mountain or an ocean. It would be a window at dusk. I would sit still and watch the light change from gold to violet, from violet to blue, from blue to the deep, patient black where stars might appear if you know how to look. I would watch the first lights turn on in distant windows, one by one, like someone opening tiny rooms inside the night.

And I would think this: we are all living inside rooms, and all our rooms have windows. We look out for comfort, for curiosity, for proof that the world is still moving when we are too tired or too sad or too still to move. We look out and say, without words, *I am here, and something out there is real.*

Maybe that is enough. Maybe that is what all writing does, too: opens a window, even if only a crack. Even if the view is small. Even if the glass is cold.

Especially then.
